name: Gajendra Varadha Perumal Temple, Kapisthalam
deity: Vishnu as Gajendra Varadha, reclining and facing east, with the Goddess Ramamanivalli (Potramaraiyal)
period: A Divya Desam of the Chola country near the Kaveri, sung by Thirumazhisai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Medieval Chola, with Vijayanagara and Nayak additions
summary: At Kapisthalam near the Kaveri, Vishnu reclines as Gajendra Varadha, the lord who came to save the elephant king — a Chola Nadu Divya Desam and one of the Pancha Krishna shrines, sung by Thirumazhisai Alvar.

sections.history: Kapisthalam, the Thirukkavithalam of the hymns, is a village near Papanasam in Thanjavur district, some twenty kilometres from Kumbakonam. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvars in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and lies in Chola Nadu, the land watered by the Kaveri. Thirumazhisai Alvar sang it in a single verse, calling the Lord 'Attrangarai Kidakkum Kannan' — Kannan who lies on the riverbank — and the shrine is counted among the Pancha Krishna Kshetrams, the five abodes of Kannan. The temple is believed to have been built by the Medieval Cholas in the late ninth century, with later contributions from the Vijayanagara kings and the Madurai Nayaks.
sections.architecture: In the Dravidian manner of the Kaveri delta, the temple gathers around a sanctum in which Gajendra Varadha lies in the bhujanga sayanam posture, reclining on the serpent and facing east. Above him rises the Gaganakruthi Vimana, the 'sky-shaped' tower. The Goddess Ramamanivalli has her own shrine. The temple's sacred waters are the Gajendra Pushkarini, named for the elephant of the legend, and the Kapila Theertham.
sections.legends: The sthala purana places here the story of Gajendra Moksha. Gajendra, king of elephants, was seized in a lotus pond by a crocodile; struggling until his strength failed, he raised a lotus in his trunk and called on Vishnu, who came at once on Garuda and set him free. Devotees say the Lord blessed both the elephant and the crocodile here. Tradition also holds that Hanuman worshipped the Lord at this place — 'kapi' means monkey, giving Kapisthalam its name — while another reading derives it from kavi, a poet.
sections.festivals: The great day is the Gajendra Moksha Lila on the full moon of Aadi (July–August), when the rescue of the elephant is re-enacted before crowds of devotees. The car festival falls on Vaikasi Visakam (May–June), and the Brahmotsavam and Vaikunta Ekadashi follow the Sri Vaishnava calendar. Confirm the year's dates with the temple.
sections.experience: Kapisthalam is a gentle village shrine whose story is easy to share with children — the elephant, the crocodile and the Lord who came running. Stand before the reclining Gajendra Varadha, then walk to the Gajendra Pushkarini. The temple combines well with the nearby Divya Desams of Thirukkoodalur and Thirupullabhoothangudi on a day's circuit from Kumbakonam.

visit.timings: Open daily for morning and evening darshan, with a midday closure; festival days are the busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering. Follow posted rules and the guidance of the priests.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow posted rules and the guidance of the priests.
visit.gettingThere: Kapisthalam is about 3 km from Papanasam in Thanjavur district, off the Kumbakonam–Thanjavur road and some 20 km from Kumbakonam. Papanasam has a railway station on the Thanjavur–Kumbakonam line; Kumbakonam and Thanjavur are the main rail towns, and Tiruchirappalli has the nearest airport.
